Confidence Interval for the Mean of a Crossed Design of Units and Raters

Source: R/ci_crossed.R
ci_crossed.Rd

The confidence interval for the population mean score of a fully crossed design, in which every rater scores every unit once, when the raters, like the units, are a sample from a population. The units are the objects of measurement (persons, essays, recordings, or the topics of an information retrieval evaluation) and the raters are whoever or whatever produces the scores (judges, coders, assessors, or automated scoring models). Because a different panel of raters would have given a different mean, the standard error carries the variability of the raters as well as of the units; treating the raters as fixed, as an interval computed from the unit means alone does, understates it whenever raters differ. This is the interval ss_aipe_crossed plans for, and its variance component rows are the planning values that function takes.

Usage

ci_crossed(ratings, conf_level = 0.95)

Arguments

ratings

A numeric matrix or data.frame with one row per unit and one column per rater, holding each rater's score of each unit. At least two units and two raters are needed, and every cell must hold a finite score: the design is complete, with no missing values. A cell may also hold a difference of two scores, as when every rater scores every unit under two conditions; the interval is then for the mean difference.

conf_level

Confidence level of the interval (default 0.95).

Value

A data.frame (class dmar_tbl) with rows ci_lower, grand_mean, and ci_upper (the estimate between its limits), se (the estimated standard error of the grand mean), df (its Satterthwaite degrees of freedom), the estimated variance components var_unit, var_rater, and var_residual (the first two truncated at zero), and the counts n_units and n_raters.

Details

Model. The score of unit \(u\) by rater \(r\) is \(y_{ur} = \mu + a_u + b_r + e_{ur}\), with independent unit effects, rater effects, and residuals of mean zero and variances \(\sigma^2_u\), \(\sigma^2_r\), and \(\sigma^2_e\); the residual holds the unit by rater interaction, which one score per cell cannot separate from error. This is the design Shrout and Fleiss (1979) call Case 2, a random sample of judges each of whom rates every target, and it is the crossed design with one random facet of generalizability theory (Brennan, 2001). The grand mean \(\bar y\) of the \(n_u \times n_r\) array estimates \(\mu\) with variance $$V = \frac{\sigma^2_u}{n_u} + \frac{\sigma^2_r}{n_r} + \frac{\sigma^2_e}{n_u n_r}.$$

Estimate and interval. With the mean squares \(MS_u\), \(MS_r\), and \(MS_e\) of the two-way analysis of variance for units, raters, and residual, the ANOVA estimates of the components are \((MS_u - MS_e) / n_r\), \((MS_r - MS_e) / n_u\), and \(MS_e\), each of the first two set to zero when it is negative. Plugged into \(V\) they give $$\hat V = \frac{k_u MS_u + k_r MS_r + (1 - k_u - k_r) MS_e}{n_u n_r},$$ with \(k_u\) equal to 1 when \(MS_u > MS_e\) and 0 otherwise, and \(k_r\) likewise for raters. The interval is \(\bar y \pm t_{\nu} \sqrt{\hat V}\), where the degrees of freedom \(\nu\) are those Satterthwaite (1946) gives for a linear combination of independent mean squares, $$\nu = \frac{\left(\sum_k a_k MS_k\right)^2}{\sum_k (a_k MS_k)^2 / \nu_k},$$ with the coefficients \(a_k\) of the numerator above and \(\nu_k\) the degrees of freedom of each mean square: \(n_u - 1\), \(n_r - 1\), and \((n_u - 1)(n_r - 1)\). The truncation keeps \(\hat V\) at or above \(MS_e / (n_u n_r)\), so it is never negative. When few raters carry a large rater component, \(\nu\) is near \(n_r - 1\) and the interval is wide: the data then hold little information about how far the mean of another panel of raters would lie from this one's.

An information retrieval evaluation. To compare two retrieval systems over topics judged by several relevance assessors (people, or automated judges such as language models), let each row be a topic, each column an assessor, and each cell the difference between the two systems' effectiveness scores on that topic computed from that assessor's judgments. The interval is then for the mean difference between the systems over the populations of topics and assessors.

Designs chosen from the data. The interval assumes the numbers of units and raters were fixed in advance, as ss_aipe_crossed fixes them, and not chosen from the data, as a two-stage sequential procedure chooses them from a pilot array.

References

Brennan, R. L. (2001). Generalizability theory. Springer. doi:10.1007/978-1-4757-3456-0

Satterthwaite, F. E. (1946). An approximate distribution of estimates of variance components. Biometrics Bulletin, 2(6), 110–114. doi:10.2307/3002019

Shrout, P. E., & Fleiss, J. L. (1979). Intraclass correlations: Uses in assessing rater reliability. Psychological Bulletin, 86(2), 420–428. doi:10.1037/0033-2909.86.2.420

See also

ss_aipe_crossed to plan the numbers of units and raters, icc for the intraclass correlations of the same array, and variance_components_mls for intervals on variance components.

Other confidence intervals: ci_proportion(), ci_proportion_paired(), ci_two_phase()

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# Shrout and Fleiss (1979, Table 2): four judges each rated the same
# six targets.
ratings <- matrix(c( 9, 2, 5, 8,
                     6, 1, 3, 2,
                     8, 4, 6, 8,
                     7, 1, 2, 6,
                    10, 5, 6, 9,
                     6, 2, 4, 7),
                  nrow = 6, byrow = TRUE)
fit <- ci_crossed(ratings)
fit
#>  term         value
#>  ci_lower     1.827
#>  grand_mean   5.292
#>  ci_upper     8.756
#>  se           1.334
#>  df           4.837
#>  var_unit     2.556
#>  var_rater    5.244
#>  var_residual 1.019
#>  n_units      6    
#>  n_raters     4    
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# The judges differ a great deal in leniency, and with only four of
# them the interval for the mean over the population of judges is wide.
# Treating these four judges as the only ones of interest ignores that
# variability; the interval from the six target means is much narrower.
t.test(rowMeans(ratings))$conf.int
#> [1] 3.532362 7.050972
#> attr(,"conf.level")
#> [1] 0.95

# The variance components are planning values for a larger study, here
# one whose 95% interval for the mean is no wider than 2 points.
v <- setNames(fit$value, fit$term)
ss_aipe_crossed(true_var_unit = v[["var_unit"]], true_var_rater = v[["var_rater"]],
                true_var_residual = v[["var_residual"]], width = 2)
#>  term               value 
#>  necessary_n_units  22    
#>  necessary_n_raters 40    
#>  total_judgments    880   
#>  cost               880   
#>  expected_width     1.997 
#>  df                 55.903
#>  rater_floor        20.146
#>  true_var_unit      2.556 
#>  true_var_rater     5.244 
#>  true_var_residual  1.019 
#>  width              2     
#>  conf_level         0.950 
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
